meta.disclaimer: Market-level observations about participants in the Australian data-centre market, built from public data. Nothing here describes any lender's exposures or counterparties.

signals.title: Hyperscaler baseline: capex ÷ operating cash flow
signals.mechanism: When capex takes more of the anchor tenants' operating cash flow, less free cash stands behind their leases.
signals.notes: Latest reported fiscal year each, ending 31 Dec 2025 (Amazon, Alphabet and Meta), 31 May 2026 (Oracle) and 30 Jun 2026 (Microsoft); the as-of is the newest year-end. In those years the five spent $464.6bn of capex against $634.9bn of operating cash flow, leaving $170.4bn of free cash flow. Their last four reported quarters of capex sum to $586.4bn; the inputs carry no quarterly operating cash flow, so the ratio stays annual.
signals.cadence: ETL lane: quarterly capex, annual statements
signals.formula: Σ capex ÷ Σ operating cash flow across Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Oracle and Meta, each at its latest reported fiscal year; the change is against each one's previous fiscal year. Per company: capex ÷ operating cash flow, FCF = operating cash flow − capex, net debt = total debt − cash and equivalents (negative = net cash), and capex summed over its last four reported quarters. Annual, not the latest quarter: the inputs carry no quarterly operating cash flow. Each fiscal year is dated by its year-end (the period of its annual capex row in quarterly_financials); the as-of is the newest of the five year-ends.
signals.chart: Latest fiscal year, per hyperscaler

signals.title: Compute commitments ÷ ARR, frontier labs
signals.mechanism: The more years of current revenue a lab's compute commitments represent, the more its leases, and any guarantee behind them, rest on growth and new funding; it moves as commitments are announced or ARR changes.
signals.notes: OpenAI and Anthropic, the labs with both series: $1,013.2bn of announced compute commitments (OpenAI at 22 Jul 2026, Anthropic at 1 Oct 2026) against $135.0bn of ARR (OpenAI at 29 Sep 2026, Anthropic at 31 Jul 2026). Three months earlier, on 1 Jul 2026, the multiple was 12.1× (commitments: OpenAI at 27 Feb 2026, Anthropic at 20 Apr 2026; ARR: OpenAI at 1 Feb 2026, Anthropic at 31 May 2026). xAI ($20.0bn committed) and Mistral ($2.3bn committed) have no ARR series, so they are in the chart and table but not the sum. Commitments are announced totals, most over multi-year terms, and ARR is one year's run rate, so the multiple reads as years of current revenue committed.
signals.cadence: On announcement; Hermes's monthly curation pass
signals.formula: Σ latest compute_commitments ÷ Σ latest arr, both USD bn from frontier_lab_valuations.csv, over the labs with both (of OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and Mistral), each lab's latest row on or before the date. compute_commitments is the lab's announced cumulative total; as_of is the newest date among the rows the sum uses. Per lab: commitments, ARR, the date each was stated, and commitments ÷ ARR. The series and the change are over the same labs: the series from the first date they all had both, the change 3 months back where they all had both then, else 1 month, else since the previous observation.
signals.chart: Compute commitments and ARR per lab, and their ratio

signals.title: Funding cadence: lab raises ÷ ARR
signals.mechanism: A lab raising more often, or more against ARR, is funding burn; its lease then rests on the runway between rounds.
signals.notes: OpenAI and Anthropic, the labs with an ARR series, raised $217.0bn in the 12 months to 08 Sep 2026 against $105.0bn of ARR. xAI ($50.0bn) and Mistral ($3.8bn) have no ARR series, so they are in the chart and table but not the multiple. The register begins 21 Jan 2025, so the multiple is drawn only for 12-month windows it covers in full; a round leaving the window moves it as much as a new one entering.
signals.cadence: Monthly curation pass (Hermes); the news catalogue carries the announcements
signals.formula: Σ USD bn raised in the 12 months to the register's newest deal (the as-of date: the newest date in funding_deals.csv) by the labs with an ARR series ÷ Σ their latest ARR on or before that date (frontier_lab_valuations.csv, metric arr). A raise is a funding_deals.csv row whose entity is OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI or Mistral AI itself and whose type is equity, debt, hybrid, debt_convertible, ipo or revolver; balance_sheet spending, acquisitions and vehicles a lab anchors (Stargate JV) are not its raises. Per lab: months from the last raise to the as-of date, the gap before it, and raise ÷ ARR at the time (the latest ARR on or before the raise date; — where there is none).
signals.chart: Raises per frontier lab, marker area = USD bn

signals.title: Guarantor concentration: largest guarantor's share
signals.mechanism: The larger the share of lease obligations one guarantor backstops, the more the market's credit rests on one name whose fortunes depend on the same demand; it moves as guarantees are announced or run off.
signals.unit: % of guaranteed value in force: NVIDIA
signals.notes: 6 guarantees in force on 17 Aug 2026, $187.3bn from 3 guarantors; NVIDIA backs $111.3bn of it. Three months earlier, on 17 May 2026, NVIDIA was also the largest, at 66.3%. A guarantee counts as in force from its announcement date until its term runs out, and without end when no term is disclosed. 1 with no term disclosed ($43.8bn, 23% of the total) is counted as in force. Amounts are as announced, not amortised over the term.
signals.cadence: Monthly curation pass (Hermes), as the funding-deal register
signals.formula: Largest guarantor's share = Σ amount_usd_bn in force of the guarantor backing the most ÷ Σ amount_usd_bn of all guarantees in force, on the register's newest date (as_of, from the date column). In force: dated on or before the date and not past date + term_years; a row with no term_years counts as in force. Amounts as announced, not amortised. The series is the largest share at each quarter end and on as_of, whoever leads on each date; the change is against the largest share 3 months before (else 1 month, else at the previous announcement). With it: Σ in force by guarantor on every date that changes (each announcement, each term end), and Σ announced by guarantor in each quarter.
signals.chart: Guaranteed value in force, by guarantor

signals.title: Circular-financing share of tracked deals
signals.mechanism: When the funder is also the customer or guarantor, one balance sheet's stress propagates through the lease; it changes how much a guarantee is worth.
signals.notes: 30 deals dated in the 12 months to 08 Sep 2026, 18 marked circular: $404.1bn of $557.4bn. A trailing window: a large deal leaving it moves the share as much as a new one entering.
signals.cadence: Monthly curation pass (Hermes); the news catalogue carries the announcements
signals.formula: Circular share = Σ amount_bn of deals marked is_circular ÷ Σ amount_bn of all tracked deals, over the 12 months to the newest deal. With it: Σ circular amount by entity and by quarter.
signals.chart: Tracked deal value by quarter, circular and not

signals.title: Listed AU operator leverage
signals.mechanism: As listed AU operators' debt to equity rises, a smaller fall in lease income strains debt service.
signals.unit: % debt to equity, median of 3 listed
signals.notes: The median of 3 ASX-listed operators' debt to equity (GMG, MAQ, NXT), each from its latest reported balance sheet, dated 28 Sep 2026 by the newest week of the price history. The quotes file is replaced on every weekly run and keeps no history, so there is no earlier value to measure a change from; net debt ÷ EBITDA and capex ÷ operating cash flow are not in the AU lane's files. Goodman's ratio is the whole group's, most of it industrial property.
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly quotes; ratios move with semi-annual statements
signals.formula: Median, across the listed operators, of debt to equity: total debt ÷ shareholders' equity, in %, from each one's latest reported balance sheet, as the AU lane's Yahoo Finance quotes carry it (NXT, GMG and MAQ at present; others as they list). Per operator with it: EV/EBITDA and market capitalisation. As of: the newest date in financials_history.parquet, written in the same run as the quotes, which carry no date. Net debt ÷ EBITDA and capex ÷ operating cash flow are not in these files, so they are not computed.
signals.chart: Listed AU operators: leverage and valuation (share prices on Company Analysis)

signals.title: Open-weights share of the cost–capability frontier
signals.mechanism: When open-weights models hold more of the cost–capability frontier, capable tokens get cheaper and cheaper tokens get used, which moves inference volume and the data-centre space it needs.
signals.notes: 105 of the snapshot's 400 models carry a GPQA score and both prices; on 02 Oct 2026, 13 sit on the frontier, 6 of them open-weights. Each quarter's frontier is rebuilt from the models released by its end at the snapshot's current prices, so a later price cut moves earlier quarters too; 6 models with an unknown licence are left out of the share and counted (0 of them on the frontier). At GPQA ≥ 75% the cheapest proprietary model, Seed 2.0 Mini at $0.175 per 1M tokens, costs 2.5× the cheapest open-weights one, GPT OSS 120B at $0.070.
signals.cadence: ETL lane: ZeroEval leaderboard pull, every one to three weeks
signals.formula: Frontier = data_llm.pareto_front over blended price ((3 × input_price + output_price) ÷ 4, USD per 1M tokens) and GPQA, of the models released up to a date that carry a GPQA score and both prices; a model priced the same as a more capable one is not a member. Open share = members whose licence is neither proprietary nor unknown ÷ members of known licence (unknown left out and counted), at the snapshot's own date (_meta.updated, the as-of) and at each quarter end. The change is against the frontier of the models released by three months earlier. Cost gap = cheapest proprietary ÷ cheapest open-weights blended price among models at GPQA ≥ 75% (cheapest_frontier's threshold).
signals.chart: Price against GPQA with the frontier, its open-weights share by quarter, and the cost gap

signals.title: $/MTok deflation at constant capability
signals.mechanism: The rate at which the price of a fixed unit of capability falls is the rate at which a tenant's revenue per token falls, so its return on leased capacity depends on volume outrunning it.
signals.notes: Cheapest at ≥ 75% GPQA on 2 Oct 2026: $0.070/MTok (GPT OSS 120B, released 5 Aug 2025); a year earlier $0.070, three months earlier $0.070, so 0.0% year on year and 0.0% quarter on quarter. No new low in the last 3 months: the 3-month change is the year-ago price leaving the 12-month window, not a new price. Each model is at its price in this snapshot and dated by release, so the line is rebuilt at every pull; the 2020–25 launch prices carry no capability score and are context only.
signals.cadence: ETL lane: ZeroEval leaderboard pull, every one to three weeks
signals.formula: P(t) = the cheapest blended price, (3 × input + output) ÷ 4 in $ per million tokens as data_llm.preprocess_ze blends it, among leaderboard models scoring at least 75% on GPQA and released by t (data_llm.cheapest_frontier's running minimum, each model at its snapshot price). Value = 100 × (P(as of) ÷ P(12 months earlier) − 1), the year-on-year change; quarter on quarter the same over 3 months. As of = the leaderboard's _meta.updated. The 2020–25 launch prices, blended the same way, carry no capability score: context on the chart only.
signals.chart: Cheapest $/MTok at ≥ 75% GPQA, log scale, against 2020–25 launch prices

signals.title: Open-weights share of OpenRouter tokens
signals.mechanism: When developers route more tokens to open-weights models, cheap inference is being used rather than just offered, which moves the volume a renewal depends on and spreads its hosting beyond the frontier labs.
signals.notes: OpenRouter is developer and aggregator traffic, not enterprise cloud volume (Azure, Bedrock, Vertex): this reads as developer mindshare, not market share. The share covers the 4 complete weeks 31 Aug to 27 Sep 2026; 11.8% of their tokens are unclassified and left out (OpenRouter's unnamed long-tail row 6.3%, codename models 2.9%, named models the map does not cover 2.7%); in the window the change is measured against, 22.7% were. The map classifies 319 OpenRouter models, 242 from ZeroEval's licence field and 77 by a stated override.
signals.cadence: Daily OpenRouter rankings pull
signals.formula: Open share = Σ total_tokens of models the map classes as open weights ÷ Σ total_tokens of models it classes as open or closed, over the 4 complete weeks (Monday to Sunday, the last ending on or before the file's newest date) to the newest complete week; 4 weeks because a single week swings 3–7 pts as models launch and fade. Unclassified tokens (OpenRouter's long-tail `other` row, codename models under stealth/ and openrouter/, and named models the map does not cover) are left out of both sides, so a codename model's launch week does not move the share, and are reported as a share of all tokens. The map, app/content/openrouter_model_map.py, gives each OpenRouter model open or closed weights and the ZeroEval model_id whose licence it was read from (proprietary → closed, unknown → not classified, any other licence → open, as R1), or an override with its reason; the leaderboard itself is not read here. Change: against the same 4-week share ending 13 weeks (3 months) earlier, else 4 weeks earlier. as_of = the newest date in the file.

signals.notes: Σ capex $477.0bn ÷ Σ cloud revenue $397.8bn across Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Oracle, 2025Q3 to 2026Q2, the newest quarter with capex and cloud revenue for all of them. 2026Q3 waits for Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet cloud revenue and capex (v_hyperscaler_capex); what is disclosed for it is in the table. Capex is as v_hyperscaler_capex records it, each company's cash purchases of property and equipment: assets taken on finance leases are not in it, and it is the whole company's, not its AI capex alone. Cloud revenue is the segment the file's notes name, so the ratio is a proxy for payback, not a return; Meta has no cloud revenue in the file and is in the table only. RPO / backlog is as each company reports it, so its scope differs: Microsoft's commercial RPO, Amazon's AWS backlog, Alphabet's Google Cloud backlog and Oracle's RPO. A few large contracts with frontier labs can make up much of a backlog; T1 (compute commitments, Frontier labs) carries them. Tokens, as the file's notes give them: Alphabet 2026Q2, “Gemini API: 22bn API tokens/minute (press release) = 31.7T/day; x30.44 days = ~964T/month”.

Per ticker, at its newest disclosed quarter: capex ÷ cloud revenue; RPO or backlog ÷ capex over the four quarters to it; the disclosed AI run-rate and tokens processed (where given). A fiscal quarter counts in the calendar quarter in which it ends. No aggregate consumer AI spend is shown: it is not observable from disclosures. as_of = the newest capex period end (v_hyperscaler_capex.period) the value uses.

signals.title: Hardware density trajectory vs tier-1 facility envelope
signals.mechanism: An option in 2040 is exercised only if the shell can house 2040's hardware; this moves when vendors' rack power and cooling needs outrun the design envelope a tier-1 operator builds to today.
signals.unit: years until the fitted trend passes 600 kW per rack

envelope.document: CDC update, Infratil Investor Day, ASX filing of 18 Sep 2025 (p. 131)
envelope.quote: CDC's cooling technologies enable cutting edge +600 kW high-density and high floor loading for advanced compute workloads.

signals.notes: The table's 4 NVIDIA rack configurations (2018–2027), fitted log-linear, grow 37% a year; the fitted trend reaches the envelope in 2028.9, and the newest row, Rubin Ultra NVL576 (Kyber rack) (2027), is stated at 600 kW per rack. The envelope, 600 kW per rack with liquid cooling, is the stated design capability of CDC Data Centres (CDC update, Infratil Investor Day, ASX filing of 18 Sep 2025 (p. 131), linked in the table: “CDC's cooling technologies enable cutting edge +600 kW high-density and high floor loading for advanced compute workloads.”), never any facility's fit-out; AirTrunk publishes no kW figure and NEXTDC's own pages disagree. One table edit so far, so no earlier value; perf per watt is on GPU Hardware & Pricing, and AMD has no row because it states no rack-level power.
signals.cadence: On vendor roadmap events; Zalen edits the table
signals.formula: Fit ln(rack kW) = a + b × year by least squares over the table's rows (one per accelerator generation: the densest rack configuration the vendor publishes; year = the availability year the vendor stated at announcement, placed at mid-year). Crossing year t* = (ln E − a) ÷ b, E = the tier-1 envelope in kW per rack. Value = t* − as_of, in years: positive is the headroom left at the fitted rate; zero or negative means the fitted trend passed the envelope that many years earlier (shown negative, never floored at zero). Change = value now − value at the previous table edit, each from the table as it stood at that edit. as_of = the date of the newest edit.
signals.chart: Rack power by generation against the tier-1 envelope

signals.title: Hyperscaler AU capital announced
signals.mechanism: Hyperscalers' stated capital and sites for Australia run ahead of their leasing; this moves when they announce, and a slowdown here would precede fewer new leases and less certain renewals.
signals.notes: 6 announcements dated 24 Oct 2023 to 28 Sep 2026, 3 with an A$ figure (A$50.0bn in all; 1 announced in the 3 months to 28 Sep 2026, adding A$0.0bn); the figures are multi-year statements of intent, some capital and operating spend together, not contracted leases. 10 site leads (tier A 5, tier B 3, tier C 2) carry no date, so they show a level, not a change. The project database has no hyperscaler flag, so the MW counted in it are those of the projects an announcement links, 550 MW in all: NEXTDC S7, 550 MW facility (Proposed), linked 05 Dec 2025.
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly rebuild of the manual seeds
signals.formula: Announced capital = Σ capex_aud_m ÷ 1,000 over every announcement dated on or before the newest announcement_date, in A$bn (an announcement with no figure is counted but adds nothing). Change = capital newly announced in the 3 months to that date. With it: the cumulative sum at each quarter end, by company; site leads counted by evidence_tier (the lead register has no date, so a level, never a change); and linked MW = facility_mw in projects.parquet of each project an announcement's linked_project names (matched on project_name, and on operator = linked_operator where a name repeats). as_of = the newest announcement_date.
signals.chart: Announced AU capital by quarter, cumulative; site leads by evidence tier

signals.title: Demand growth needed to fill the risked pipeline
signals.mechanism: Renewals are negotiated against spare capacity when filling what can actually be built needs faster demand growth than the published scenarios; this moves when projects advance or drop out, or the scenarios are revised.
signals.notes: NEM regions: 38 operating projects record 1,641 MW (25 more disclose no MW and add nothing); the pipeline to 2032 is 2,001 MW risked of 6,908 MW unrisked; the pipeline outside the NEM (WA, 200 MW risked) shows only by region. full_capacity_year is recorded for 1 of 27 NEM pipeline projects, so 15 are placed by startup_year and 11 undated ones (378 MW risked) at 2032; as AEMO notes new facilities take five to ten years to reach a mature rate, the comparison is made at 2032, not year by year. PUE 1.32 is the median of the 49 NEM projects with MW that state one; at AEMO's 45–51% the needed growth is 24.3–26.6% a year, and on the 2025 actual the operating stock runs at 21% (AEMO: 27% of connection capacity in quarter 1 2026). No earlier value: the project database keeps no vintages and the scenarios are fixed.
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly rebuild of the project DB
signals.formula: Needed growth = (D ÷ A)^(1 ÷ (H − Y)) − 1, in % a year. A = the latest actual NEM data-centre consumption (TWh in Y, the last Baseline year of dc_demand_forecasts.csv); H = the last year all three scenarios reach; D = the TWh that would run the operating stock plus the pipeline dated by H at a mature utilisation: D = Σ MW × k × u × 8,760 ÷ 10^6, over NEM regions (NSW1, QLD1, VIC1, SA1, TAS1). MW = risked_mw (the project database's existing risk weights; risk_base_mw for the unrisked case); k = PUE for MW recorded as IT load or a campus envelope, 1 for MW recorded as facility power (capacity_basis power_consumption_mw, gross_power_mw, grid_connection_mva). u = 50%: AEMO's mature-fleet utilisation of connection capacity (AEMO, 2026 ESOO (Aug 2026), p. 36: 45–51% by data-centre type, around 50% in aggregate; 45% and 51% are shown too: https://www.aemo.com.au/-/media/files/electricity/nem/planning_and_forecasting/nem_esoo/2026/2026-electricity-statement-of-opportunities.pdf?rev=4f2e73fbd906456288198fdbc24b335a&sc_lang=en). PUE = the median pue of the NEM projects with MW that state one (value and count in the notes). A pipeline project (any status but Operating) is placed at its full_capacity_year, else startup_year, else H, and no earlier than Y + 1; one dated after H is left out. Each scenario: growth = (its TWh in H ÷ A)^(1 ÷ (H − Y)) − 1, and utilisation = its TWh ÷ the TWh of the stock plus pipeline at full use. The scenarios are national, so regions are a breakdown, not compared one by one; the regional ESOO supply surplus is not used, as its maximum demand already includes AEMO's own data-centre forecast. as_of = the newest last_verified_at in projects.parquet.
signals.chart: Demand needed at mature use vs the scenarios (NEM, TWh); MW by region

signals.title: Pre-commitment ratio: share of capacity contracted
signals.mechanism: Capacity built against signed contracts carries renewal risk, and capacity built on spec lease-up risk first; this moves when operators sign contracts or add capacity, and a falling share is an early sign of oversupply.

operators.geography: Global portfolio with Sydney project line

signals.notes: Contracted 1,000 MW against 2,906 MW of capacity for the one operator disclosing both, CDC Data Centres (capacity stated 08 Apr 2026, contracted 06 May 2026): each operator's latest figure of each kind, paired. It states 21.5% of the 13,525 MW of capacity in the seed (8 of 11 operators give a figure, each on the geography it states); NEXTDC's contracted 667 MW has no capacity figure here. No earlier value: no earlier date in the seed has these operators disclosing both.
signals.owner: Hermes (curates the seed); AU lane rebuilds
signals.cadence: Semi-annual: operator results and valuations
signals.formula: Per operator: contracted_capacity_mw ÷ (operating_capacity_mw + under_construction_mw + future_build_mw), a blank part counted as 0, or ÷ total_capacity_mw where the row gives no breakdown; each operator's latest dated contracted figure is paired with its latest dated capacity figure. Market figure = Σ contracted ÷ Σ capacity over the operators with both, in %. Disclosing share = their capacity ÷ the capacity the file states across all its operators (each operator's latest figure). as_of = the newest announcement_date among the rows the market figure uses. The change is since the previous point, over the same operators.
signals.chart: Contracted and stated capacity, by operator

signals.title: Power-secured share of announced pipeline
signals.mechanism: Only pipeline with secured power can become supply competing with leased sites at renewal; this moves as announced projects secure power, and a low share means announced competition is softer than its headline MW.
signals.unit: % of Proposed + Approved MW; 33% not recorded
signals.notes: 17 Proposed or Approved projects stating 5,354 MW: 756 MW (14.1%) with power recorded as secured, 2,815 MW (52.6%) recorded as not secured and 1,784 MW (33.3%) with no record either way, so the secured share would be 47.4% if every unrecorded project had power. MW is each project's stated capacity (facility_mw), which mixes IT load and site power envelopes, campus full-build figures included, as the sources give them. The date is the newest last_verified_at among these projects; projects.parquet keeps no earlier vintages, so there is no change to show yet.
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly rebuild of the project DB
signals.formula: Secured share = Σ MW of Proposed and Approved projects with power_secured = true ÷ Σ MW of all Proposed and Approved projects, national, in %. MW per project = facility_mw (the database's stated capacity), else critical_it_mw, else it_load_mw; a project with none is counted as without a figure and adds no MW. power_secured empty (not recorded) is neither true nor false: its MW stays in the denominator and is shown beside the share, with the share if all of it were secured. By region: secured, not secured and not recorded MW per nem_region. as_of = the newest last_verified_at of those projects. No change yet: the file keeps no earlier vintages.

signals.title: AI-workload share of the AU pipeline
signals.mechanism: The more capacity is built for AI, the more its renewals rest on AI inference economics; this moves as AI campuses are announced or start operating, and sizes how far the renewal signals reach.
signals.notes: Pipeline (Proposed, Approved and Under Construction): 29 projects stating 7,253 MW, 5,720 MW of it (78.9%) AI/HPC or Cloud/AI, of which Cloud/AI, a mix of AI and cloud, is 432 MW. Operating stock: 70 projects, 41 of them stating 1,672 MW, 3 MW of it (0.2%) AI; the other 29 state no MW, counted and adding nothing, so the operating share covers only the projects with a figure. MW is each project's stated capacity (facility_mw), which mixes IT load and site power envelopes, campus full-build figures included; every project records a workload type. The date is the newest last_verified_at; projects.parquet keeps no earlier vintages, so there is no change to show yet.
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly rebuild of the project DB
signals.formula: AI share = Σ MW of pipeline projects whose workload_type is AI/HPC or Cloud/AI ÷ Σ MW of all pipeline projects, in %; pipeline = every status but Operating (Proposed, Approved, Under Construction). Beside it, the same share of operating stock (status Operating). Cloud/AI mixes AI and cloud workloads and is counted as AI, shown on its own in the table. A project with no workload_type is its own class (not recorded), never Traditional, and is not AI. MW per project = facility_mw (the database's stated capacity), else critical_it_mw, else it_load_mw, as S3; a project with none is counted as without a figure and adds no MW. By region: MW per workload class per nem_region, operating and pipeline. as_of = the newest last_verified_at. No change yet: the file keeps no earlier vintages.
signals.chart: Workload mix of operating and pipeline MW, by region

signals.title: Grid-connection queue (US proxy)
signals.mechanism: The longer a new data centre waits to energise, the longer incumbents with connected power hold their pricing at renewal; a shorter queue or wait means competing supply arrives sooner.

avg_wait_time_years.source: Rand et al. (2024) UChicago/LBNL queue analysis [DERIVED]

signals.notes: US queue depth for 2024 is 2,290 GW (LBNL Queued Up 2025 Edition, published 15 Dec 2025), 310 GW less than for 2023; the newest US Avg Wait Time is 4.0 years (2024). LBNL reports the wait from connection request to commercial operation as a median for a build cohort, and each edition's cohort differs, so a change between editions mixes cohort and method. LBNL counts generation and storage seeking a US grid connection, not data-centre load: a proxy for connection friction. The AU queue is S4-AU, beside it on this dossier.
signals.cadence: Annual: LBNL Queued Up edition (Hermes curates the file)
signals.formula: Queue depth = the United States 'Queue Depth' row (GW of generation and storage seeking a grid connection, LBNL Queued Up) for the newest year in dc_queue_metrics.csv, read from the newest edition where a later one restates the year. Change = that minus the previous year's figure, since the previous year's published_date. Beside it: the United States 'Avg Wait Time' rows (years from connection request to commercial operation; the spec's 'median time-to-COD', the file's name kept). ERCOT and PJM Interconnect rows are listed in the table, not charted: single-market figures from other sources, not comparable with the national series. as_of = the published_date of the queue-depth row the value uses.

signals.title: Grid-connection queue, NSW1
signals.mechanism: The longer a new data centre waits for a grid connection in Australia, the longer incumbents with connected power hold their pricing at renewal; a shorter queue means competing supply arrives sooner.

signals.notes: NSW1 queue at 30 Jun 2026: 4,680 MW (AEMO QED Q2 2026: NSW 52% of the 9.0 GW NEM total (derived)), 1,440 MW more than at 31 Mar 2026 (AEMO QED Q1 2026: NSW 60% of the 5.4 GW NEM total (derived)). A queue counts capacity applied for and not yet connected, as its source counts it; a change of source between dates moves the series without the queue moving. The NEM-wide median wait, 547 days at 30 Jun 2026 (AEMO NEM Connections Scorecard June 2026: generation & storage connections, NEM-wide, not data-centre load), counts generation and storage connections, not loads; AEMO publishes no load figure. The US proxy (S4) is on this dossier beside it.
signals.cadence: Quarterly: AEMO Quarterly Energy Dynamics and NEM Connections Scorecard (Hermes curates the file)
signals.formula: Queue depth = the NSW1 queue_depth_mw row (MW applied for and not yet connected, AEMO Quarterly Energy Dynamics) at its newest date in connection_queue.csv; change = that minus the previous NSW1 figure, since its date. Beside it: each region's queue depth and median_days_to_connect (median days from application to connection, AEMO NEM Connections Scorecard), charted for NSW1, QLD1, VIC1, SA1 and TAS1; other rows, such as the NEM total, are tabled. GW, months and years are converted to MW and days. as_of = the newest NSW1 queue_depth_mw date.

signals.title: Delivered power price, NSW1
signals.mechanism: Power is passed through to the tenant, so a rising delivered price lowers the tenant's return on the site and is the lever it pulls at renewal.
signals.notes: NSW1, 365 days of prices in the 12 months to 31 Aug 2026: wholesale A$75.0/MWh; no network row is in force for NSW1, so this is wholesale alone. A rolling year, so the winter peak does not read as a change; each region's latest full quarter against the same quarter a year earlier is in the table. NSW1's last bar, 2026 Q3, is a partial quarter, 62 of its 92 days; a partial quarter's bar is drawn lighter.
signals.cadence: AU lane: weekly NEMOSIS pull of AEMO's monthly archives
signals.formula: Delivered price = wholesale (AEMO regional reference price, RRP) + the network charge in force (AER, where published), A$/MWh. Each region's rows are averaged by calendar day first; a network row applies from its date until the region's next one. Headline: NSW1, the mean daily delivered price over the 12 months to the newest price date; change = that minus the same 12-month average three months earlier. Beside it: quarterly averages by region, wholesale and network stacked, and each region's latest full quarter against the same quarter a year earlier (YoY). as_of = the newest NSW1 wholesale date.

signals.title: Regulatory changes reaching existing assets
signals.mechanism: This moves when a regulator or government applies a network charge, levy, operating obligation or planning condition to data centres already built, which raises the cost of running them under leases already signed.
signals.unit: of 10 items in 12 months reach existing assets

items.instrument: Improving the NEM access standards – Package 2 (ERC0394): draft rule determination
items.summary: Draft rule sets a tiered framework for applying access standards to large loads, with new disturbance ride-through and instability standards for large inverter-based loads such as data centres.

items.instrument: Expectations of data centres and AI infrastructure developers
items.summary: Five national expectations, including that new data centres secure new clean energy to offset their demand and cover their share of network costs; Commonwealth assessments prioritise the proposals most closely aligned.

items.instrument: Powercor distribution determination 2026–31, Attachment 16 (connection policy): final decision
items.summary: Load customers newly connecting at 22 kV or above, which includes most data centres, pay the tax on their type 1 capital contributions upfront.

items.instrument: AI in Australia's interests: Australian Standards for AI (announcement)
items.summary: Announces standards, expected to be legislated in early 2027, under which large data centres would underwrite their own new power supply, pay their full share of connection costs and reduce power when needed.

items.instrument: Operational integration and visibility of large inverter-based loads (ERC0455): rule change request
items.summary: Asks the AEMC for rules on operational visibility, monitoring, communication and information sharing for large inverter-based loads such as data centres.

items.instrument: Data centre energy obligation: advice to Energy and Climate Change Ministers
items.summary: Recommends that data centres offset their consumption with certificates from new renewable generation, contract for firming capacity and meet market registration requirements, with demand flexibility supported through connection agreements.

items.instrument: Reforming electricity network connection and cost recovery arrangements for data centres in NSW: consultation paper
items.summary: Ten proposed reforms for data centres of 15 MW or more, including an entry bond, a Major Network Upgrade Fee, contributions to jurisdictional scheme costs from transmission-connected data centres and information obligations on proposed and existing connections.

items.instrument: NSW Data Centre Policy Framework and NSW Data Centre Guidelines
items.summary: Six principles for data centre projects, including investment in additional water and energy supply; projects that meet the performance measures are assessed within 75 days.
Would require new data centres to bring their own renewable supply and storage, meet connection and network upgrade costs, cool with recycled or non-drinking water and keep 150 metres from homes.

items.instrument: Cost recovery for network augmentations – Packages 1 & 2 (ERC0448, ERC0456): consultation paper
items.summary: Consults on the Minister's requests that data centres and other large loads pay the network costs they cause, including prudential requirements, transmission-level recovery of jurisdictional scheme costs and a public register of large loads.

signals.notes: 10 items in the register, 10 of them dated in the 12 months to 2 Oct 2026, its last review: 2 that apply to existing facilities or connections as their sources state, 5 to new developments or connections only and 3 whose sources say neither. Items include proposals, consultations and announcements as well as made rules; the instrument column gives each one's stage. 2 such items are dated after 2 Jul 2026. The register was last reviewed on 2 Oct 2026, after its newest item (24 Sep 2026), so it is dated by that review.
signals.cadence: On event; Hermes's monthly curation pass
signals.formula: Count = items in regulatory_register.csv with affects_existing = yes, dated in the 12 months to as_of (as_of − 365 days < date ≤ as_of). affects_existing is what each item's source says: yes where it says the instrument applies to existing facilities or connections, no where it says new or expanded developments or new connections only, unclear where it says neither. as_of = the later of the register's newest item date and its last review (fetcher_log.json, regulatory_register.last_run; the newest item alone when that record is missing or unreadable). Change = the count at as_of less the count three months earlier (one month when the register does not reach back three). Series: the count at each quarter end and at as_of. Chart: one mark per item by date, in a lane per affects_existing reading (categorical colours, unclear in grey), with the 12-month window shaded.
